1:
Ellicott objects that these two verses are not the beginning of anything, since in the Hebrew they still belong to the section before, and that the chapter division obscures both their sequence and their point. On his reading they answer the case just legislated for, of an Israelite driven by poverty to sell himself to a heathen and so obliged to live among idolatrous practices, and Gill reports that Jarchi and Aben Ezra had already connected them that way, though he prefers to treat the law as a principal one standing on its own account. Henry finds the placing natural for a different reason, that a master who has given many charges ends by repeating the ones his servant is likeliest to neglect. Keil and Delitzsch set the whole chapter in a larger frame, that the book of the covenant had closed with promises and threats about conquering the land and these close the law at Sinai with promises and threats about holding it.

Ellicott separates the three prohibited things carefully, an image which may represent the God of Israel quite as much as a heathen deity, a pillar which was a plain unworked stone and had once been raised to God himself, and a figured stone. Clarke reaches the same point from history, that the stones anointed by holy men to commemorate God's interpositions were later abused, so that what had been innocent was forbidden, exactly as happened to the brazen serpent. Wesley states the qualification plainly, that a pillar was not simply prohibited, since holy men set them up both before this law and after, but only a pillar meant to be bowed down to. Gill glosses the word for idols as things of nought, since an idol is nothing in the world, and takes the graven image to cover the molten kind afterwards worked with a tool, as the golden calf was.

Henry explains why this sin above others provokes God, that after his being and unity we must know him to be an infinite Spirit, so that to make an image, to consecrate it, and to bow to it changes his truth into a lie and his glory into shame. He adds the melancholy observation that no sin was more provoking and none they were more addicted to. Ellicott reports what the second Temple made of the figured stone, that it meant a stone set in the ground for worshippers to prostrate themselves upon, a signal drawing the eye to itself. On that reading the Temple pavement was lawfully figured while such stones were forbidden elsewhere, which is how the Chaldee paraphrase and the old canon divide the case.

Both Henry and Ellicott treat the second command as the safeguard of the first, Ellicott that a man who keeps the sabbath will effectually guard himself against idolatry, and Henry that sabbaths and reverence for the sanctuary are the instrumental part of religion by which the essentials are kept up. Henry notes that the prophets reprove the Jews for profaning the sabbath more often than for anything except idolatry itself. Wesley defines the reverence required as purging the sanctuary from uncleanness and conducting its services only in the manner God appointed. Henry closes the introduction on the difference between human law and divine, that governments enforce their statutes by penalties while God will be known as the rewarder of those who seek him.
3:
Ellicott holds that this verse, not the two before it, begins the section in the Hebrew and ought to have begun the chapter in English, the legislator closing by showing what obedience brings and what transgression. Gill reads the statutes as moral, ceremonial and judicial together, all now recorded in this book and the one before, since the two that follow are chiefly repetition. Calvin fastens on the condition and concedes its difficulty, since what God promises on the terms of our walking in his commandments would be ineffectual if he examined our works strictly. His answer is that the deficiencies of believers are put out of sight by faith and their imperfect efforts rewarded as if the duty had been discharged. To walk in the commandments is therefore not to perform whatever the law demands but to be indulged as a son who serves, which exposes the pride of those who imagine they make God their debtor.

Calvin adds that the confining of the recompense to this transitory life belongs to the elementary instruction of the law, reconciliation and reward alike being represented to that people by visible things. He presses this against those who infer from God's present silence that his nature has altered, and against the Manichean who makes the God of Israel another. Gill and Clarke agree that the rain in due season is the former and the latter, and Ellicott dates the early rain from mid-October to December and the vernal to March and April. Wesley draws the moral that God placed them in no land watered by a Nile but in one dependent on the rain of heaven, keeping that key in his own hand to bind them to obedience.

Calvin observes that God might have promised abundance in one word, but names the instruments instead, so that the seasons should renew the memory of his bounty daily. Clarke, following Pliny, sets the Judaean calendar beside the Egyptian, where the people were shut up in their cities three months by the inundation, and quotes Dodd for a plenty so entire that harvest and vintage leave no interval. Gill and Ellicott date the threshing from March and the vintage from July, Ellicott adding sowing time in October, and both cite Amos on the ploughman overtaking the reaper. Gill takes the promised peace of broils and civil wars among themselves, Ellicott of lying down without fear of robbers; Ellicott also complains that the Authorised Version renders the same Hebrew about evil beasts differently here and in Ezekiel. Keil and Delitzsch explain lying down unafraid from a flock at rest, and treat the multiplying of the nation as the covenant carried forward toward completion.

Ellicott calls five chasing a hundred a proverb for a handful outmatching a regiment, and Wesley that five is a certain number put for an uncertain. Calvin alone finds a difficulty, that none making them afraid and their chasing of enemies do not agree, and resolves it by the wars still to be fought for the land. Clarke takes the tabernacle set among them for the grand promise of the gospel, since John says the Word made his tabernacle among us; Calvin insists the visible sanctuary was no empty sign, and finds in I will be your God the hope of immortality that Christ drew from those words. Keil and Delitzsch, hearing satisfied repose in the word for dwelling, deny that God's walking refers to his leading them on their journeys and refer it to his presence in Canaan itself, where Gill and Wesley read it of the pillar of cloud and fire. Ellicott closes with the appeal to the deliverance, explaining the broken bands from ox harness, the rods across their necks leaving the beasts helpless before the driver; Wesley glosses the upright walk as heads lifted and not pressed down.
14:
Ellicott marks the turn, the glowing promises being followed by a catalogue of calamities of the most appalling nature, the first degree of which runs to the seventeenth verse. Calvin explains why threats are added at all, since thus far the invitation has come in the shape of promises, obedience being approved by God only when willing. He states the objection against himself, that one compelled by fear will never love God, and answers that threats serve the children of God differently, preparing them to fear before regeneration and subduing their corrupt affections after it. Keil and Delitzsch insist that the judgments follow not from single breaches but from contempt of all the laws, and Henry likewise excludes sins of ignorance and infirmity, for which sacrifices were provided.

Henry traces the descent by steps, from carelessness and omission to a despising of the statutes that thinks meanly of the law and the Lawgiver, then to abhorrence, since those who turn from religion turn against it, and last to disowning the covenant. His note on that step is that the covenant is God's, who made it, while the breach is man's, so that God must have all the honour and man all the blame. Ellicott finds the same gradation in the grammar, and would drop the word but before the breaking of the covenant, since it is the abhorrence of the law that breaks it, better rendered thereby breaking my covenant. Gill sets out the ladder plainly, negligent hearing bad, not doing worse, contempt worse still, while Wesley reads the clause as breaking their part and thereby discharging God from the blessings promised on his.

Calvin alone narrows the description, holding that it applies only to ungodly apostates who deliberately revolt, since one who falls through infirmity or offends from inconsideration is not said to have despised God's law. He concedes that all transgressors fall under the curse, and that God speaks of gross rebellion here to show the lengths to which those proceed who assume the liberty of sinning. Clarke stops at the words despise my statutes and abhor my judgments to take a general view of the terms for the divine law, twelve of them, each traced to its root. Statutes he derives from a verb meaning to mark out and define, judgments from one meaning to distinguish and regulate, commandments from the act of a legislator binding by penal sanction, and covenant from a root meaning to cleanse, because the revelation was to separate that people and make them holy; testimonies, ordinances, precepts, truth, righteousness and the word of Jehovah follow, and the law itself from a verb meaning to set straight and true, as stones in a building.

Henry reads the setting of God's face as God setting himself to ruin them, since proud sinners he will resist, or else takes the face for anger; Gill makes it the exerting of his power, the reverse of the respect promised above. Clarke sees the evils personified and appointed as governors over a disobedient people, and challenges the deist to compare the chapter with the state of the Jews since Vespasian. Henry takes appoint over you of taskmasters ruling with rigour, reports bishop Patrick's guess that the terror is the falling sickness, and puts all chronic diseases in the consumption and all acute in the burning ague, which Wesley repeats almost word for word. Ellicott presses three renderings, smitten rather than slain, rule rather than reign, and extinguish the eyes rather than consume them, since consume misleadingly echoes the consumption just named, and he asks that this passage and Deuteronomy be made uniform, the same word appearing as burning ague here and simply fever there. Henry adds that those who hate them shall rule over them justly, since they were not willing that the God who loved them should reign.
18:
Calvin reads the gradation itself as mercy, God chastising lightly those whose hardness he has not yet proved and adding severity only when obstinacy is added. He cites Paul on those who take occasion from God's forbearance to heap up vengeance, and David's warning not to be as the horse or the mule, the one remedy being teachableness. Ellicott counts the degrees, this verse opening the second, the third running through the wild beasts and the fourth to the twenty-sixth, which Keil and Delitzsch likewise call stages. On the sevenfold measure they divide, Keil and Delitzsch taking seven as the number of perfection and so the chastisement at full height, while Ellicott and Calvin agree that it fixes no number but stands for an indefinite many.

Gill reports that the Targum of Jonathan and Jarchi understood the pride of their power of the sanctuary, broken first by Nebuchadnezzar and then by the Romans, though he prefers the land or their forces. Ellicott confirms that the second Temple read it so from the same phrase in Ezekiel, and complains that the Authorised Version hides the identity by rendering it the excellency of your strength; Wesley includes ark and sanctuary with the kingdom and the armies. Keil and Delitzsch make it everything on which a nation rests its might, and Calvin finds in it men whom prosperity has made secure, Israel waxing fat and kicking as horses grow restive by overfeeding. Ellicott notes that Deuteronomy threatens the same thing with the metals reversed.

Calvin devotes a long note to the word rendered contrary, which the Chaldee takes of hardness, as though they purposed to contend with God, and Jerome renders in opposition to me. Because the root signifies an accidental occurrence he prefers to walk at adventures, that is, to pass by God's judgments with the eyes shut and ascribe adversity to fortune. Gill offers both senses, and when the word is turned upon God takes it either of open enmity or of God behaving with indifference, as if everything came to them by accident. Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch keep the hostile sense, the one making it continued defiance, the other glossing the idiom as going to meet a person in enmity.

Clarke collects the fulfilments of the wild beasts, the fiery serpents, the lions sent among the settlers in Samaria and the bears that tore the children, and adds Ainsworth's reading of them as tyrants and false prophets who devour souls. Gill allows the same double sense, literal beasts or the monarchs of Assyria and Babylon, while Ellicott stays with the literal. Keil and Delitzsch add that with the cattle destroyed and the people made few the highways would cease for want of travellers. On the sword Calvin insists that all wars are stirred at God's command, who calls the Assyrian his axe and Nebuchadnezzar his soldier, so that Israel's troublers executed his vengeance. Ellicott would render it simply the sword that avenges my covenant, Wesley glossing the quarrel as God's quarrel with them for breaking it.

The last threat divides them sharply. Ellicott, Clarke and Wesley read the ten women at one oven as scarcity, one oven sufficing for ten families where ordinarily it served one, the bread returned by stinted weight. Calvin argues the contrary, that Moses means abundance and no fraud in the baking, the women coming together so that each may see whether due weight is given, the curse lying in this alone, that the staff being broken they eat and are not satisfied. He grounds it on the doctrine that man lives not by bread but by the command of God, and compares the staff to the stick on which the old and weak lean. Gill and Keil and Delitzsch take the broken staff of a famine, and Ellicott sets beside it Ezekiel's bread by weight and water by measure.
27:
Ellicott introduces the fifth and last warning, threatening the total destruction of land and people, the words in fury being added to the earlier formula as the provocation grows. Gill gathers the fulfilments of the threat that they should eat their own children, the sieges of Samaria and Jerusalem, and the woman Mary at the last siege, whose story Clarke and Ellicott take from Josephus, as does Calvin. The act would be incredible were it not attested, and Calvin gathers from it how terrible it is to fall into the hands of God.

Gill reports that Jarchi took the high places for towers and palaces and Aben Ezra for places of sacrifice, while Ellicott, granting that such eminences also served the worship of Jehovah, holds that the context requires idolatrous ones, and renders the images sun-pillars. He makes the casting of their carcases upon their idols one heap of contempt for worshipper and god alike, while Wesley thinks the idols are called carcases to mark them lifeless, or to show them broken beside those who trusted them. Calvin takes the same gesture as God's finger pointing out his abhorrence of their worship, in which apostates delight until he appears as its avenger. On the refusal to smell their sweet odours Calvin observes that the phrase embraces all the expiatory rites their confidence in which had made them obstinate, and Wesley presses the possessive, the sanctuary called theirs and not God's because he disowns what they defiled.

Ellicott marks a change of agency, the earlier devastations being invasions God permitted, while the desolation of the country and the dispersion are his own work, at which their very enemies will be astonished. He observes the exact reversal of the promise, the sword that was not to go through their land being now drawn by God himself to pursue them out of it, and adds that not even the sanctuary is spared, God undoing his promise to dwell in their midst. Gill reads the scattering as a winnowing with the fan.

Clarke reports Houbigant's computation as historical proof, that from Saul to the captivity are some four hundred and ninety years, containing seventy sabbaths of years, and that the captivity lasted exactly seventy; he infers that the law was kept until Saul's time, or the exile would have run longer. Calvin explains that God joined the land with man in the sabbath to increase reverence for it, and reproves the people for defrauding even the ground, which groaned under such inhabitants; the only way left to honour him there was to empty it, an extorted rest put in the room of the voluntary one. Ellicott likewise has the land making up by its long fallow the sabbaths of which it was deprived, but Keil and Delitzsch deny the debt, holding that sabbath-keeping never bound the land and that the verb means to enjoy rest, not, with Gesenius and Knobel, to pay what is owed.

Gill describes the survivors falling over one another in their hurry, and rejects the Jewish reading that each falls for his brother's iniquity because all Israel are sureties for one another. Calvin takes this last vengeance to be the lingering death of those who escaped the sword, God filling their hearts with trembling so that they flee unpursued and start at a falling leaf, which he judges worse than being cut off at a blow. Ellicott insists that perish is better rendered be lost, since the next verse speaks of a remnant, and explains the land eating them up as their being so absorbed among the nations as to disappear. Gill reports Rabbi Akiba applying this to the ten tribes, and Clarke asks the same. On the pining away he would read because of their iniquity rather than in it, and gives the Chaldee rendering, that they pine for their fathers' sins which they hold fast.
40:
Henry says the chapter closes with gracious promises of returning favour upon repentance, that they might not despair unless by their own fault. Calvin makes the point more sharply, that Moses addresses not sinners in general but those who by obstinacy have come nearest to vengeance, mercy being offered to the worst of men. He adds that this favour belongs by special privilege to the Church, the cause assigned being that God will remember his covenant, which the fallen must seize as shipwrecked sailors seize a plank. Gill, Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch agree that the clause reads better as prediction than condition, and they shall confess rather than if they shall confess.

Henry finds three marks of the repentance required, confession, godly sorrow and submission to God's justice, and requires that they confess the wrath as well as the sin. He notes that sin is put under its worst character, as walking contrary to God, and that the unhumbled heart is called uncircumcised, the mark of a Gentile stranger rather than an Israelite in covenant. Calvin runs through the same fruits and distinguishes the confession meant from the kind exacted under the papacy, in a priest's ear. He observes that naming the fathers magnifies the guilt, and warns that following them does not extenuate a child's fault but makes it less excusable.

On accepting the punishment of their iniquity they part. Ellicott would render it accept willingly, the verb being the one translated enjoy of the land's sabbaths, so that they take their punishment joyfully as the fittest means to repentance. Wesley reads it as acknowledging God's righteousness and their own wickedness and submitting patiently, saying with David that it was good to be afflicted. Calvin rejects both senses, observing that the noun means iniquity and punishment alike and the verb to expiate or appease, and renders it let them atone for their iniquity, by allusion to the sacrifices.

Ellicott takes remember in its sense of perform, and observes that the word covenant is repeated before each patriarch, from which the second Temple concluded three distinct covenants, located by the Chaldee at Bethel, Moriah, and between the divided pieces. He notes that this is the solitary place where the order of seniority is inverted, which Henry accounts for as an ascending line beginning with Jacob and leading back to the most ancient promise, made to the father of the faithful. Henry adds that God remembers the covenant when he performs it purely for his own faithfulness, and Calvin insists that for their sakes means for their profit and not their merit. Clarke observes that though the threatenings were fulfilled in the loss of land, polity, city and temple, providence has preserved that people distinct and numerous, and looks for all Israel to be saved and folded with the Gentiles under one Shepherd, while Wesley reports the comfort the Jews take from the place.

The closing formula divides them over its reach. Gill refers it to all the preceding chapters of the book, and gives the Targums, which read that the laws were made between his Word and Israel. Ellicott confines it to the statutes begun in the previous chapter, since it ends with the phrase it began with and so forms a section by itself, while Keil and Delitzsch make it the close of the covenant legislation from Exodus onward. Clarke treats it as the proper end of the book and conjectures that the chapter following once stood before it, a column of the parchment roll having been displaced, though he allows that it may have been added later. Henry closes on the law as the bond of communion, God showing not only dominion but favour in giving it and the people not only holy fear but holy love in keeping it, so that it stands rather as a covenant than a law, a sentence Wesley repeats almost exactly.
